epitaph: The LDA brand's own title, created when the WWA briefly split into three brands (Meltdown/NWC, Fiesta/LDA, and SCWF) in 2004. Jack Griffiths won the first Diablo reign on 17 May 2004, surviving a hectic singles bout against Odium and then four more men in a cage-match final; Odium took the belt back from Griffiths one show later, on 14 June 2004, in a match the fed's own title-history ledger never recorded. The lineage ends with the fed's own words: Odium — "the second Diablo Champion," by his own farewell — left the WWA on 11 August 2004, and five days later the belt was folded into the Extreme Championship's relaunch, never defended again.

events.note: Folded into the WWA Extreme Championship's 16 Aug 2004 relaunch, per that show's own main-event billing ("unified the DIABLO and GenX Titles" / "the NEW and FIRST WWA Extreme Champion"); the last champion had left the fed five days earlier per its own news post.

name: Diablo Championship

epitaph: Opens under "WWA GenX" billing, its first champion "Sky Flyin" Jimmi Zion crowned 7 March 2003 in a title unification with the Cruiserweight Championship — but Zion already held the Extreme belt itself at that point, having won it solo from an untraced "Rage In A Cage 6" after a brief joint reign with Chance, who in turn had won it back from Enigma in a 2-on-1 handicap match on 6 January 2003; Enigma took the belt clean off Chance on 9 December 2002. Chance's own reign before that loss, and Shaman's own four reigns predating Chance's (billed on-air, December 2002 and again February 2003, as "Four time former WWA Extreme Champion"), remain a genuine, honest gap — no opponents or dates for either survive in the recovered corpus. The belt's own recap prose shifts to "Extreme Championship" branding by early 2004 without a break in the numbered ledger. "Bonafide" James Curzon, Shaman, and Jonathon Winters all held it more than once across the run; the title was folded into the Television Championship on 26 March 2006, "merged with the TV Title" in the ledger's own words, before Eddie Van Dorn and Tarin Ballard closed out the fed's final recovered Extreme-title reigns in 2007.

events.note: The FWA's own Hardcore Championship folded into this belt when Shaman defeated FWA Hardcore Champion The Dehibilitator in a title-unification match three and a half weeks after the rest of the FWA was absorbed into the WWA's own banner at Independence Day Rumble (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-28.html).

name: WWA Extreme Championship
notes: The fed's own numbered ledger (title id 9) traces this belt continuously from an earlier "Gen X Championship" billing to the "Extreme Championship" name, with no break in the sequence — only the champion's own billing changes mid-record.

epitaph: Created as "the major title on the Fiesta brand" on 21 July 2003, defended only a handful of times in the surviving record before Mal Somers's reign closes out the fed's own recovered ledger on 26 July 2004.
name: WWA Intercontinental Championship

epitaph: A developmental title for the fed's own newer talent, active from at least 1999 and repeatedly retired and reinstated across the surviving record — "the Rookie Ring is retired, once again" reads one of its own ledger entries, followed months later by a full relaunch. Mal Somers's win over Barrett Sinclair at Birthday Brawl 2002 closes out the fed's final recovered reign.
name: WWA Rookie Championship

epitaph: The fed's own numbered ledger for this belt runs continuously from an early "European Championship" naming (its first tournament winner, The Psycho, crowned 12 April 2003) through 4 March 2004, when Rocky Adams's win is recorded, in the fed's own words, as making him "the last ever EWA Champion and the first ever SCWF Champion" — the same night the European Wrestling Alliance closed and the Squared Circle Wrestling Federation launched from its ashes. Armaan took the belt from Adams on 21 March 2004, carrying the first SCWF Championship into the brand's later absorption back under the unified WWA banner.
name: SCWF Championship
notes: The fed's own numbered ledger (title id 7) traces this belt continuously from an earlier "European Championship" billing to the "SCWF Championship" name, with no break in the sequence — only the champion's own billing changes mid-record. Its earliest surviving row (Desolation, stripped of a pre-existing reign "while still holding the championship" upon his promotion to the WWA roster) predates the belt's own numbered start and carries a corrupted source date; no WWA-side win is recorded for that reign, so it is not counted among these rows.

epitaph: Contested from the fed's earliest recovered years under the New York City Championship name — a New York City Title tournament crowns Randy Cross champion at the RIC Athletic Complex on 21 November 1997, and its own served card explicitly bills the belt as "the New York City Title" straight through Johnny Blaze's own steel-cage title win a fortnight later. WWA's own later title-history ledger folds this same lineage into the "WWA Television Championship" retroactively, dating Cross's own tournament win to 14 November 1997 — a week earlier than the served card's own internal dateline ("Friday, November 21, 1997"), and the served show is preferred here as the stronger primary source (see the reign's own note). From there the belt passed through dozens of hands across the surviving record to the 2008 rebuild; Nicholas Adams's own bio credits him with four reigns, more than any other champion in the title's history, and the belt saw multi-time runs for Mantis, Shaman, and Vik Ventressa.

events.note: The FWA's own Television Championship folded into this belt when Lyle Wile defeated FWA Television Champion Chad Goodman in a title-unification match at Independence Day Rumble, the same FWA-absorption card (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html).

name: WWA Television Championship

epitaph: A secondary singles title running alongside the World Heavyweight Championship from the fed's own earliest recovered years, contested under the New England Championship name in WWA's own NCW predecessor era — Johnny Blaze wins it in an over-the-top battle royal the served card bills as "the CWC New England Championship Title" on 2 January 1998, the same event WWA's own later title-history ledger folds into "WWA United States Championship" retroactively, and is billed "the New England Champion" on the fed's own served card of 9 January 1998. From Blaze's ledger-tracked win the title ran on, held across long runs by Steihl, Tracer Bullet (three times), and Grunge, whose 6 June 2003 – 30 November 2003 reign is credited in his own bio page as the longest in the title's history.

events.note: The FWA's own North American Championship folded into this belt when Buck Floyd defeated WWA United States Champion Shawn Cage in a title-unification match at Independence Day Rumble, the same FWA-absorption card (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html).

name: WWA United States Championship

epitaph: Crowned at WWA's own 12/12/97 founding tournament, when Mark Lynch outlasted the field to become the fed's first champion — a tournament the served card itself bills throughout as "the CWC Northeast Heavyweight Championship," WWA's own later title-history ledger folding it into "WWA Championship" retroactively from this exact reign. From Lynch's own coronation the belt changed hands dozens of times across WWA's continuous run, carried by four-time champion Tracer Bullet, two-time champions Damian Thorne, Craven Moore, and Armaan, and a seven-month reign for Ian Tense rivaled only by Nik Segier's own early run. The fed's own last recovered capture (September 2010) leaves Trendkiller as champion, having just outlasted RJ Stone, Jack Griffiths, Chris Bagwell, and Jaymz Watkins inside the Ultimate Glory match.

events.note: The FWA's own World Heavyweight Championship folded into this belt when Jim Black, arriving from the FWA, defeated WWA World Heavyweight Champion Nik Segier in a title-unification match at Independence Day Rumble — the same card that saw the FWA absorbed into the WWA's own banner (promotions/wwa/archive/2000-07-02.html; data/frontier.json's FWA (Colosseum/Loge/2603) row).

name: WWA World Heavyweight Championship

epitaph: Defended across dozens of pairings from 1998 onward, including four-time champions The Veteranz and a run for The Franchise Players (Tracer Bullet and Denrol). The fed's own title history has the front office retire the belt on 1 May 2003; it was revived exactly one month later, on 1 June 2003, when Havoc defeated X-Corp for the reinstated title, and continued changing hands for years afterward.

events.note: The fed's own ledger: "Matt Warr, in his infinte wisdom retires the WWA World Tag Team Titles." Revived one month later, 1 June 2003, when Havoc defeated X-Corp for the reinstated title.

name: WWA World Tag Team Championship

epitaph: Never tracked on the fed's own title-history ledger, and inconsistently billed by the fed's own broadcasts as the "Light Heavyweight" and "Cruiserweight" Championship in different shows of the same era (Eddie Van Dorn — same man, same weight, same hometown billing — defends it as "Cruiserweight" on 4 March 2002 and loses it as "Light Heavyweight" on 15 April 2002, then immediately calls himself "the Cruiserweight champion" in the very next breath as the new champion — the same belt, not two). The surviving record opens on Tuesday Showdown, 22 February 2000, where the reigning champion Mystique lost it to Denrol in a lumberjack-style main event after Denrol swapped places with a disguised Pitt Viper — the show's own commentary crowned the win as making Denrol the WWA's first-ever Grand Slam Champion, not the belt's own first titleholder. "Sky Flyin" Jimmi Zion was champion by the earliest served 2002 shows; Eddie Van Dorn won it from him off-panel before 25 February 2002 and held it through a 4 March 2002 defense, before Trent LeBeaux (wrestling as Tracer Bullet under his own registered ring name) beat him for it in the 15 April 2002 Monday Night Meltdown main event. Grunge took it from LeBeaux on 12 August 2002, the belt's own last confirmed change in the recovered record. Ramsey Kaine stole it from Grunge with a cheated rollup on 23 September 2002, then no-showed his own next defense; the fed restarted the match as a straight bout between the two men who did turn up, and EkoSyde beat Grunge for it on 7 October 2002. EkoSyde -- unmasked on-air as Enigma, who also held the WWA Extreme Championship at the same time -- lost it in a 2-on-1 handicap match on 6 January 2003, where the referee, unable to award a single champion, named Chance and "Sky Flyin" Jimmi Zion joint champions of both belts at once -- the belt's own last change directly staged in the recovered record. A later show (10 February 2003) refers back to Jimmi Zion having won the belt outright from Chance at an untraced "Rage In A Cage 6," ending the joint reign; that PPV itself was never captured, so the win is reconstructed from the later show's own retrospective billing rather than a staged title change. The belt's own end is dated precisely, even though its middle stretch isn't: Commissioner Raine retired it on-air on 8 March 2003's Fiesta, unifying it with the Extreme Championship into the new WWA GenX Championship, with Zion's own unified reign dated a day earlier in the fed's own ledger. One clean pre-2000 change is now recovered: Jak "The Boil" Lancer lost the title to Griffin (wrestling masked as "Lone Wolf") in an I Quit match on wwa-1998-11-08 — Lancer's own preceding win date remains unrecovered.

events.note: Retired on-air by Commissioner Raine and unified with the Extreme Championship into the new WWA GenX Championship.
events.title: wwa-extreme

name: WWA World Light Heavyweight Championship
note: Recovered from show text (e.g. archive/2000-02-22.html, archive/2002-01-28.html, archive/2002-04-15.html), not WWA's own titles.php ledger — the only title in this shard sourced that way. Other served shows (1998-08-21, 1999-04-24, 1999-06-25, 1999-08-13, among others) reference this same belt by name with other apparent pre-2000 holders (Jak "The Boil" Lancer, Griffin, Nik Segier); it also keeps getting referenced under the "Cruiserweight" billing across a large share of the rest of the 2002 corpus (archive/2002-06-17.html onward through at least 2002-12-21.html). A fuller lineage on both ends is real, evidenced, and not yet reconstructed; flagged for a future dedicated pass rather than guessed at here.

epitaph: A singles championship of NCW/WWA's own 1997–98 predecessor era, referenced directly in the promotion's own broadcast voice as early as 12 December 1997 (the winner of the CWC Northeast Heavyweight tournament billed as "probably the number one contender") but never staged for or defended within any show read so far. Its first confirmed holder is museum-compiled from a single announcer line: Darken is credited as CWC National Champion (alongside the New England and National/Northeast Tag titles) on 9 May 1998, with no won-date, prior challenger, or staged match surviving in the held record.
name: CWC National Championship

epitaph: A tag title of NCW's own predecessor era, already held by Darken and Steihl (the Overlords of the Dark) on the fed's own served card of 9 January 1998 — no won-date or prior challenger is recoverable, and no title defense survives in the held record.
name: CWC National Tag Team Championship

epitaph: Minted for an 8-man single-elimination tournament staged at the RIC Athletic Complex in Providence, Rhode Island, across two shows (20 and 27 Feb 1998) — Johnny Blaze wins the inaugural championship, submitting House of Pain's Zack Crockett in the final.
name: CWC Rhode Island Championship

epitaph: A short-lived 1998 title, crowned via a dedicated tournament (semifinals wwa-1998-12-26, final wwa-1998-12-27) and won outright by New Star. Not confirmed to be the same lineage as the modern wwa-extreme title (whose own epitaph traces its recovered ledger continuously only from 2003's "GenX" billing, with no mention of an earlier belt) — filed as a distinct, likely-discontinued early incarnation rather than merged, absent evidence tying the two.
name: WWA Extreme Hardcore Wrestling Championship
